stories.headline: Japan issued a 9.9 magnitude earthquake alert, but ground didn't shake: What happened
stories.title: Japan issued a 9.9 magnitude earthquake alert, but ground didn't shake: What happened
stories.summary: An "alert" indicating a massive magnitude-9.9 earthquake sent shockwaves of fear across Japan on Friday afternoon. Just eight minutes after its issuance, the Japan Meteorological Agency retracted the warning, which had been triggered by a lesser magnitude-6.9 quake off the Kamchatka Peninsula in Russia. Although the alert caused temporary disruptions in transportation, officials are now investigating the warning system to ensure public safety and prevent future confusion.

stories.headline: Farooq Abdullah slams IAS officer over misconduct, demands his removal from J&K
stories.title: Farooq Abdullah slams IAS officer over misconduct, demands his removal from J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 16: National Conference president Dr Farooq Abdullah on Friday said he felt ashamed after watching a video of an IAS officer misbehaving with a woman officer, calling his conduct unbecoming of a senior administrative official. Speaking to reporters in Srinagar, Dr Farooq Abdullah, said the language used by the officer was unacceptable and reflected a lack of the discipline and professionalism expected of an IAS officer. “The language he used with the woman officer was extremely inappropriate. He should be reprimanded. This shows that he lacks the manners and conduct expected of an officer,” he said, as per the news agency—Kashmir News Observer (KNO). Dr Farooq said officers were appointed to serve the public, listen to their grievances and resolve their problems rather than insult or humiliate them. “People want to express their grievances, and officers should hear them patiently. Instead, he directly said, ‘Get out, get out.’ This is completely wrong. He should be removed from Jammu and Kashmir,” he said. Expressing dismay over the incident, Abdullah said, “When I saw the incident on social media today, I felt ashamed. His behaviour was completely unbecoming of an IAS officer. He has put the entire administrative community in an embarrassing position.” Asked whether such incidents occurred during his tenure as Chief Minister, Abdullah said no officer or minister had the right to insult people. “Whether someone is an officer or a minister, they are here to serve the people and resolve their difficulties, not to insult or abuse them,” he said. Backing Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s remarks that such an incident would not have occurred had Jammu and Kashmir retained its statehood, Farooq Abdullah said he would have taken stronger action against the officer. “He would not merely have been attached. He would have been thrown out. If I had been in office, he would not have remained in Jammu and Kashmir for more than a few minutes. I would have put him back on a plane and sent him away,” he said. He said the incident reflected changes in the administrative functioning of Jammu and Kashmir since 2019. On protests in Delhi, Abdullah welcomed the demonstrations, saying a new wave was emerging against what he described as autocracy. “I think these protests are very good. A new wave is beginning against autocracy and against a Hitlerian way of life,” he said. Dr Farooq futher urged US President Donald Trump to recognise dialogue and negotiations as the only viable means of resolving disputes. “Let us hope that Trump realises that war is not a solution. Negotiation is the way to resolve conflicts. You are not going to win through war. You will only end up killing people, and innocent people will lose their lives,” he said.—(KNO)

stories.headline: How Indian space tech startups are going global and attracting foreign capital
stories.title: How Indian space tech startups are going global and attracting foreign capital
stories.summary: In October, just three months after becoming the first private Indian space tech startup to launch a rocket in space, Skyroot is fielding enquiries from abroad about its launch vehicle Vikram.“Seventy to 80 percent of the demand we are seeing is global,” says Pawan Chandana, its co-founder and CEO.Most enquiries have been from the US, Europe and Southeast Asia. In October, Skyroot teamed up with Brazil’s Concert Technologies to jointly develop a 100-kg low Earth orbit launch vehicle, while also securing a deal with US-based Reflect Orbital to deploy future spacecraft across two dedicated launches.This global interest is matched by a surge in foreign capital. Not just in Skyroot.Also Read: Beyond ISRO: Meet 5 Indian Space Startups Making Global Headlines in 2026Pixxel, a Bengaluru-based startup that works on Earth imaging satellites, closed a $100 million round in September, the largest the sector has seen, led by global investment firms Temasek and Seraphim. The company was also the first Indian space tech startup to raise from a global investor when Canada’s Radical Ventures led its Series A, and in 2023, Google made its first ever investment in an Indian space tech startup by leading Pixxel’s $36 million Series B. In 2021, Agnikul Cosmos, a launch vehicle startup, raised $11 million in a Series A round led by Mayfield India, the India-focussed arm of US-based Mayfield.Indian startups are also embedding themselves into foreign markets. Digantara, a space surveillance and intelligence company, has established a manufacturing and operational footprint in Denver, Colorado, purpose-built to service US government and defence contracts. Its other such facility abroad is in Singapore.Beyond drawing foreign capital and sewing up foreign contracts, India’s space tech startups are also building unique technologies. GalaxEye became the first Indian space tech startup to secure a landmark US patent for its OptoSAR in September, a proprietary dual-sensor technology that integrates optical and radar observation. This does not exist anywhere else in the world and is getting interest from clients in West Asia.The task now is to convert this attention into commercial success, mass production, and, eventually, sustainable global market share. The upside is huge. The global space economy is put at $630 billion, according to an estimate by World Economic Forum and McKinsey & Company in 2023, and the US accounts for most of it, followed by China, Europe and Japan. India accounts for less than 2 percent, with its space tech sector estimated at $8.4 billion.Also Read: How Skyroot Aerospace Became India’s First Spacetech UnicornGlobal PlayIndia opened up its space sector to private participation long after the US and Europe did. However, this does not faze Pawan Goenka, chairman of IN-SPACe, a government agency for promoting private space tech industry. “Our companies are quite aggressive in wooing customers outside India,” he says, adding that India’s startups are winning orders from abroad and “will be very competitive in two to three years”.IN-SPACe data shows that only half of India’s top 10 space tech companies lean heavily on the home market. MistEO gets all its orders from domestic entities, Suhora and GalaxEye above 90 percent, Digantara 80 percent, and Bellatrix more than 70 percent.The other five look outward. Dhruva Space gets 90 percent of its business from abroad and HEX20 80 percent. Agnikul describes most of its orders as international and Skyroot says its book is predominantly foreign. Piersight sits in the middle, with half of its business being international.Firms selling launch vehicles and launch-linked services skew global, while those that depend on Indian government and defence customers stay anchored at home. The overseas orders are mostly for hardware and engineering services rather than data. They include satellite structures, solar panels, propulsion systems, and full satellites and design work, which suggests Indian startups are winning abroad as low-cost, space-qualified suppliers.Companies focussed on data and analytics find that orders from overseas require more than hardware exports.Pixxel, for instance, is building a physical presence in the markets where it sells. It has a subsidiary in El Segundo, California, which CEO Awais Ahmed credits with winning the Nasa and National Reconnaissance Office contracts—a $476 million Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme, giving the hyperspectral imaging startup a route to supply Earth observation data to the US space agency till November 2028.A European subsidiary is “on the verge”, Ahmed says, with West Asia and Southeast Asia to follow. The European national governments, the EU and the European Space Agency have all raised their budgets, he says, creating room for unique space products such as hyperspectral imagery. Revenue, he argues, should be diversified not only between government and commercial customers but also across governments. What gets Pixxel through the door, he adds, is technology no one else offers at that resolution, “because if you are just replicating something that someone else has already done, it becomes difficult”. Pixxel is also planning to go public soon, Ahmed says.Mark Boggett, CEO of Seraphim, the global venture capital firm dedicated to space tech which led Pixxel’s record funding round in September, frames Pixxel’s model as a template for Indian startups to transition from being domestic players to competing globally. He points out how it “has built significant technology and manufacturing capabilities in India while establishing operations in the US, giving it access to customers, talent and capital in the world’s largest space market”. Boggett predicts that the next five to 10 years could be decisive, and that India’s engineering talent, government ambition and growing private funding will “create the conditions for companies to emerge that can compete globally”.Also Read: How startups are battling the odds to launch a new space tech age for IndiaThe World KnowsDigantara’s international strategy focuses on Asian markets first. It set up a wholly owned subsidiary in Singapore in 2022 and used the city state as a gateway to Asia-Pacific, finding clients in Thailand and Japan. Anirudh Sharma, CEO of Digantara, says India’s Ministry of External Affairs has helped open doors in places such as the Philippines and Mongolia, where Digantara wants to site ground sensors. Madagascar is next. “These countries are so small that no big company will look at them,” he says, “but they are good enough markets for us to start with.”It is not a bad start. Digantara has gone on to hold US government contracts for space situational awareness and missile defence, and bought a 30,000 square foot facility in Denver; the company’s facility in Bengaluru spans 50,000 square feet.“Most of the US government customers, including the Pentagon, know of us and have worked with us,” says Sharma, adding that these are multiple contracts ranging from building payloads to designing algorithms, from software to building a spacecraft.Digantara’s American subsidiary is staffed by US citizens and operates independently of its Indian parent; it is run day to day by US citizens who make operational decisions. This helps it work with US government customers and comply with rules on foreign access to sensitive technology.Also Read: Why the success of Vikram-1 matters more than the rocket itselfThat is a requirement of the work and also a limit. “We cannot have any control over the entity… it has to be an independent entity with no influence from India because we work on national security for the US government,” Sharma says.Skyroot’s Chandana says clients from Europe and Southeast Asia, in addition to the US, are creating demand across Earth observation, communications, Internet of Things (IoT), climate and weather monitoring, technology demonstrations, and other emerging small-satellite applications. “The larger opportunity for Vikram (Skyroot’s small satellite rocket) is around dedicated and responsive access to space. Many small-satellite operators today have to fly as secondary payloads on larger rockets. That can mean waiting for availability and compromising on the timing or precise orbit they require,” he explains. Echoing the need for reliable access, Reflect Orbital Co-founder and CEO Ben Nowack says, “There’s a real launch capacity shortage right now. We’re excited to work with a new launch provider, Skyroot, to help ensure access to space.”Chennai-based Agnikul’s Srinath Ravichandran describes a quieter European presence. Agnikul has signed Memorandums of Understanding (MoU) with European players. “We have announced a few of these publicly,” he says of the MoUs with Finnish company ICEYE for launching synthetic aperture radar Earth observation systems from India, and with France’s Safran in June. “Some others are still confidential.”His company plans to fly its reusable Agnibaan rocket in 2027 and has seen interest from imaging satellite operators in Europe and Australia, and from communications operators in Europe, Japan and Australia. Ravichandran describes a shift in how overseas buyers see India. “The world knows that we know what it means to build space-grade systems,” he says, a reputation he credits to Isro’s decades of work.Other companies have taken different routes.Also Read: India can aim to be the No. 1 space power: Pixxel CEODifferent OrbitsBellatrix says 85 to 90 percent of its revenue is exports, mostly to European customers. Its propulsion systems are bought by constellation operators planning multiple satellites, none of which can function without a propulsion system. Rohan Ganapathy, co-founder, CEO and CTO, says the startup is also looking east, not just geographically but also with an entirely new piece of hardware. Its push into Asia bets on a new satellite built for very low Earth orbit (VLEO), where hardly anyone has managed to stay up.It has a collaboration with South Korea’s Telepix, an imaging firm, to fly a wide-swath camera in VLEO, around 200 km above Earth. The orbit is unusual because it is where satellites normally cannot stay. At that height the atmosphere is thin but not empty, and the nitrogen particles in it create a drag that pulls a satellite down.Ganapathy explains that a satellite that would last five to seven years at 500 km above Earth would exhaust its conventional fuel supply in just four months if it is 300 km lower. But flying closer to Earth makes images sharper, with resolution improving by four to nine times over today’s optical satellites. The lower exposure to radiation means satellites can use cheaper commercial electronics instead of space-grade parts. And it avoids the crowded orbits above 500 km, which Ganapathy likens to real estate where slots are hard to get.And so, Bellatrix’s fix is to turn the problem into a fuel. At its manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, scientists and engineers have developed electric thrusters to use the thin atmosphere’s nitrogen as propellant, which in theory lets a satellite stay up as long as they want.It was this combination that drew in Telepix. The Korean company makes cameras for satellites and approached Bellatrix, after it announced its VLEO plans, to fly its camera and offer services. A launch is planned for 2027, after technology demonstrations later this year. “When we start as a business, we always focus on Europe or the US. We tend to forget the Asian side of things. But even Asia is a very big market in itself,” says Ganapathy.Confidence in EcosystemYashas Karanam, co-founder and COO at Bellatrix, says the logic is partly commercial. “The real reason we are looking into this market (Asia) is because a lot of the Western technologies have not penetrated there, so they don’t have as much US or European supplies. And that is a good opportunity for India because we have good tech these days, and the costs are significantly better,” he explains.Bellatrix is also talking to clients across Australia and West Asia for more future contracts. Other Indian startups are finding their own unique pathways abroad.Hyderabad-based Dhruva Space has expanded its footprint beyond India through high-profile European partnerships. It has partnered with French operator Kinéis for IoT space assets, teamed up with Finland’s synthetic aperture radar leader ICEYE for full-stack space solutions, and infrastructure projects and satellite programmes with Thales Alenia Space in France and Italy.In Asia-Pacific, Dhruva has a partnership with Japan’s Infostellar for ground segment services and with Australian startup Esper Satellites for cross-border payload hosting. Its most recent LEAP-2 mission, in October, featured a star tracker built by France-based Sodern (ArianeGroup) alongside an Indian payload from Satleo Labs. “That confidence is coming in into the ecosystem that the technologies being built in India and the capability to deliver space missions from India are reliable,” says Keyur Gandhi, director, Space Regulatory and Commercialisation for Dhruva Space.However, expanding into foreign markets is also a country-specific exercise with structural barriers. Sharma of Digantara says Europe is the hardest to break into. Funding there is routed through national space agencies and the European Space Agency, with contracts returned to companies in the contributing countries. To access it, a company needs to be majority-owned by a European. Defence funding from the EU and NATO has a similar 51 percent ownership requirement. Strict employment laws make it risky to build a team on a trial basis.Selling through PartnersFor GalaxEye, which makes satellites that combine optical and radar imaging, the foreign route runs through resellers. CEO Suyash Singh says most of the startup’s customers are channel partners that sell on to their own governments, not governments buying directly. The startup’s US patent for the OptoSAR technology, he says, has helped those partners. “A lot of global customers” have come forward since the grant, he says, and some who were at the “letter-of-intent stage have signed contracts”. The contracts begin paying once the satellite is in orbit.These clients, which are based in West Asia and Europe, are mainly buying OptoSAR for dual-use purpose, particularly after the war in West Asia broke out earlier this year and also, as Singh put it “because the budgets for defence are too much”. Interest among players in West Asia was already there, Singh says, but “it has accelerated quite a bit now”.The patent has also changed the questions buyers ask, he says. Foreign customers once wanted to know who was building the technology and whether the team had done it before. “Those things are now going away gradually,” Singh says. He says that foreign customers have begun to treat India as a source of original technology and not only of cheaper versions. “The [international] customers have started to believe now that the real technology innovations can really come out of India,” adds Singh.The company’s satellite, Mission Drishti, was lost about two months after launch in May. Even so, Singh says none of the resellers, including the government’s commercial arm NSIL and about 20 partners worldwide, retracted from their contracts. They told him they would restart the clock when the next satellite reaches orbit, planned for early 2028. The cost is that GalaxEye’s plan to expand into America is on hold. With its satellite not operating, Singh says, a US subsidiary is about a year and a half away, though discussions still continue.For its part, the team at GalaxEye is still trying to establish contact with its OptoSAR satellite three months after solar flares cut-off communication.When an Indian space company wins foreign orders, its suppliers share in the gain, though it arrives in stages.Vishwanathan Hariharasubramanian, co-founder and director of Valence Advanced Materials, which makes process materials used to manufacture carbon-composite parts and is a supplier to Skyroot, says his company’s growth is tied to its customers. As Skyroot builds even bigger rockets, Valence’s supply grows with them.The Real TestPixxel’s Ahmed says India’s space tech startups have found gaps rather than replicated existing technology. One is trying optical, another hyperspectral, and two or three are on radar. It is not dozens doing the same things that are already being done in the US or China.GalaxEye’s Singh says Indian companies are strikingly consistent. Delegations from France, Japan, the Netherlands, Australia and the US visiting Bengaluru’s Space Expo six years apart saw largely the same firms still working on the same problems. Bellatrix’s Rohan adds that the constraints of India’s market have made engineers creative in cutting costs.The challenges are just as consistent.Capital, especially for higher funding rounds, remains a concern, and heftier growth cheques largely come from abroad. While government customers are slower and fewer than in the US, launch capacity is uncertain, and there are critical components India cannot yet make, such as the expensive semiconductor chips.Several founders say Indian companies have not marketed themselves internationally. Bellatrix’s Karanam says there are two kinds of companies: Those which are technically serious and market-aware and those “blinded by confidence” whose fundraising outpaces their execution.In niches where Indian technology is distinctive, such as Pixxel’s hyperspectral data, GalaxEye’s fused sensor, Bellatrix’s thrusters, Digantara’s space awareness, Skyroot’s small satellite launch vehicle or Dhruva Space’s space engineering solutions, customers abroad are paying or signing up.In launch, the gap with the US and China is real, and Skyroot’s second Vikram will show whether first-flight success can be repeated. “Our immediate focus is on establishing repeatability and progressively increasing launch cadence. The opportunity is significant because globally there are still more satellites looking for dedicated launch opportunities than there is available launch capacity,” says Chandana.Beyond engineering, Boggett says, the businesses that keep attracting capital will be “those that can translate great technology into large, repeatable revenues”. Gandhi from Dhruva Space says India needs to “now look at solving the challenge for infrastructure financing through debt and grant funding for both building infrastructure on ground for space; and building infrastructure in space for ground”.Ahmed, meanwhile, has a piece of advice for Indian space tech companies looking to scale up. “One thing we can probably be doing better,” he says, “is looking international from day one.”

It has a collaboration with South Korea’s Telepix, an imaging firm, to fly a wide-swath camera in VLEO, around 200 km above Earth.
The orbit is unusual because it is where satellites normally cannot stay.
At that height the atmosphere is thin but not empty, and the nitrogen particles in it create a drag that pulls a satellite down.
But flying closer to Earth makes images sharper, with resolution improving by four to nine times over today’s optical satellites.
The lower exposure to radiation means satellites can use cheaper commercial electronics instead of space-grade parts.
And it avoids the crowded orbits above 500 km, which Ganapathy likens to real estate where slots are hard to get.
And so, Bellatrix’s fix is to turn the problem into a fuel.

At its manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, scientists and engineers have developed electric thrusters to use the thin atmosphere’s nitrogen as propellant, which in theory lets a satellite stay up as long as they want.
It was this combination that drew in Telepix.
The Korean company makes cameras for satellites and approached Bellatrix, after it announced its VLEO plans, to fly its camera and offer services.
A launch is planned for 2027, after technology demonstrations later this year.
“When we start as a business, we always focus on Europe or the US.
We tend to forget the Asian side of things.
But even Asia is a very big market in itself,” says Ganapathy.
Confidence in EcosystemYashas Karanam, co-founder and COO at Bellatrix, says the logic is partly commercial.
“The real reason we are looking into this market (Asia) is because a lot of the Western technologies have not penetrated there, so they don’t have as much US or European supplies.
And that is a good opportunity for India because we have good tech these days, and the costs are significantly better,” he explains.
Bellatrix is also talking to clients across Australia and West Asia for more future contracts.
Other Indian startups are finding their own unique pathways abroad.
Hyderabad-based Dhruva Space has expanded its footprint beyond India through high-profile European partnerships.

It has partnered with French operator Kinéis for IoT space assets, teamed up with Finland’s synthetic aperture radar leader ICEYE for full-stack space solutions, and infrastructure projects and satellite programmes with Thales Alenia Space in France and Italy.
In Asia-Pacific, Dhruva has a partnership with Japan’s Infostellar for ground segment services and with Australian startup Esper Satellites for cross-border payload hosting.
Its most recent LEAP-2 mission, in October, featured a star tracker built by France-based Sodern (ArianeGroup) alongside an Indian payload from Satleo Labs.

“That confidence is coming in into the ecosystem that the technologies being built in India and the capability to deliver space missions from India are reliable,” says Keyur Gandhi, director, Space Regulatory and Commercialisation for Dhruva Space.
However, expanding into foreign markets is also a country-specific exercise with structural barriers.
Sharma of Digantara says Europe is the hardest to break into.
Funding there is routed through national space agencies and the European Space Agency, with contracts returned to companies in the contributing countries.
To access it, a company needs to be majority-owned by a European.
Defence funding from the EU and NATO has a similar 51 percent ownership requirement.
Strict employment laws make it risky to build a team on a trial basis.
Selling through PartnersFor GalaxEye, which makes satellites that combine optical and radar imaging, the foreign route runs through resellers.
CEO Suyash Singh says most of the startup’s customers are channel partners that sell on to their own governments, not governments buying directly.
The startup’s US patent for the OptoSAR technology, he says, has helped those partners.
“A lot of global customers” have come forward since the grant, he says, and some who were at the “letter-of-intent stage have signed contracts”.
The contracts begin paying once the satellite is in orbit.

These clients, which are based in West Asia and Europe, are mainly buying OptoSAR for dual-use purpose, particularly after the war in West Asia broke out earlier this year and also, as Singh put it “because the budgets for defence are too much”.
Interest among players in West Asia was already there, Singh says, but “it has accelerated quite a bit now”.
The patent has also changed the questions buyers ask, he says.
Foreign customers once wanted to know who was building the technology and whether the team had done it before.
“Those things are now going away gradually,” Singh says.
He says that foreign customers have begun to treat India as a source of original technology and not only of cheaper versions.
“The [international] customers have started to believe now that the real technology innovations can really come out of India,” adds Singh.
The company’s satellite, Mission Drishti, was lost about two months after launch in May.
Even so, Singh says none of the resellers, including the government’s commercial arm NSIL and about 20 partners worldwide, retracted from their contracts.
They told him they would restart the clock when the next satellite reaches orbit, planned for early 2028.
The cost is that Galax.
Eye’s plan to expand into America is on hold.
With its satellite not operating, Singh says, a US subsidiary is about a year and a half away, though discussions still continue.
For its part, the team at GalaxEye is still trying to establish contact with its OptoSAR satellite three months after solar flares cut-off communication.
When an Indian space company wins foreign orders, its suppliers share in the gain, though it arrives in stages.

Vishwanathan Hariharasubramanian, co-founder and director of Valence Advanced Materials, which makes process materials used to manufacture carbon-composite parts and is a supplier to Skyroot, says his company’s growth is tied to its customers.
As Skyroot builds even bigger rockets, Valence’s supply grows with them.
The Real Test.
Pixxel’s Ahmed says India’s space tech startups have found gaps rather than replicated existing technology.
One is trying optical, another hyperspectral, and two or three are on radar.
It is not dozens doing the same things that are already being done in the US or China.
Galax.
Eye’s Singh says Indian companies are strikingly consistent.
Delegations from France, Japan, the Netherlands, Australia and the US visiting Bengaluru’s Space Expo six years apart saw largely the same firms still working on the same problems.
Bellatrix’s Rohan adds that the constraints of India’s market have made engineers creative in cutting costs.
The challenges are just as consistent.
Capital, especially for higher funding rounds, remains a concern, and heftier growth cheques largely come from abroad.
While government customers are slower and fewer than in the US, launch capacity is uncertain, and there are critical components India cannot yet make, such as the expensive semiconductor chips.
Several founders say Indian companies have not marketed themselves internationally.
Bellatrix’s Karanam says there are two kinds of companies: Those which are technically serious and market-aware and those “blinded by confidence” whose fundraising outpaces their execution.
In niches where Indian technology is distinctive, such as Pixxel’s hyperspectral data, Galax.

Eye’s fused sensor, Bellatrix’s thrusters, Digantara’s space awareness, Skyroot’s small satellite launch vehicle or Dhruva Space’s space engineering solutions, customers abroad are paying or signing up.
In launch, the gap with the US and China is real, and Skyroot’s second Vikram will show whether first-flight success can be repeated.
“Our immediate focus is on establishing repeatability and progressively increasing launch cadence.
The opportunity is significant because globally there are still more satellites looking for dedicated launch opportunities than there is available launch capacity,” says Chandana.
Beyond engineering, Boggett says, the businesses that keep attracting capital will be “those that can translate great technology into large, repeatable revenues”.

Gandhi from Dhruva Space says India needs to “now look at solving the challenge for infrastructure financing through debt and grant funding for both building infrastructure on ground for space; and building infrastructure in space for ground”.
Ahmed, meanwhile, has a piece of advice for Indian space tech companies looking to scale up.
“One thing we can probably be doing better,” he says, “is looking international from day one.”

It set up a wholly owned subsidiary in Singapore in 2022 and used the city state as a gateway to Asia-Pacific, finding clients in Thailand and Japan.

Skyroot’s Chandana says clients from Europe and Southeast Asia, in addition to the US, are creating demand across Earth observation, communications, Internet of Things (IoT), climate and weather monitoring, technology demonstrations, and other emerging small-satellite applications.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court today stayed the ongoing trial before a Bhopal sessions court in the unnatural death case of Twisha Sharma.

A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi issued notice to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), her husband Samarth Singh and mother-in-law Giribala Singh on a plea by her father seeking transfer of the proceedings from Madhya Pradesh to Delhi.
Advocate Abhijeet Sinha appeared Twisha's father Navnidhi Sharma.

He has sought the transfer due to an apprehension that the case would not receive a fair trial in Madhya Pradesh because Giribala Singh, one of the accused, is a former judge and is influential in the state.

The CBI subsequently took over the probe.
Twisha, a 33-year-old woman, was discovered dead at her matrimonial home in Bhopal on May 12, 2026, around five months after her marriage to Samarth Singh on December 9, 2025.
Her husband, Samarth Singh, a lawyer, and mother-in-law, Giribala Singh, a retired district judge, are facing prosecution in the case.

The initial FIR was registered under Sections 80(2) (dowry death), 85 (cruelty by husband or his relatives) and 3(5) (common intention) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), along with Sections 3 and 4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act, which deal with giving or taking dowry and demanding dowry, respectively.

The order balances medical needs with strict security, access and cost conditions.

The Supreme Court on Friday allowed Popular Front of India founding chairman E Abubacker, who was arrested in a case under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, to undergo treatment at a Delhi hospital, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
The court imposed several conditions, including that Abubacker bear the cost of his treatment and the police escort.
It also allowed one family member to accompany him.
A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale directed that Abubacker be treated at Max Super Speciality Hospital in Saket.
The bench asked the hospital to submit a report on the further treatment required and the possible duration of his stay.
"The petitioner shall also pay requisite charges for escort.

Cost of hospital shall be borne by the petitioner," the bench said.
Justice Sundresh orally observed that the court could not be insensitive to such matters, adding that as a judge, "you have to mix it with some sympathy".

At the Pathways to Viksit Bharat Conclave, MoSPI Secretary Saurabh Garg explained why India periodically updates its GDP measurement framework to reflect structural changes in the economy. He highlighted how the expanding digital economy, new products and services, and data sources such as GST, e-Vahan and the Public Financial Management System can improve estimates of economic activity. Garg noted that revisions can push estimated GDP higher or lower, depending on improved data coverage and methodology. India is also working to strengthen validation mechanisms and align national accounting with the international System of National Accounts. The discussion included areas being examined for possible incorporation by 2029 - 30. What could this mean for India’s growth numbers?

The arrangement seeks to resolve protocol disputes while leaving project grievances to authorities.

The Supreme Court on Friday directed Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra to inform the Nadia district administration a day before visiting the district so that necessary arrangements, including accommodation according to protocol, can be made, news agency Press Trust of India reported.

The court issued the direction while hearing Moitra's plea against a September 1 circular that required MPs and MLAs to give the district administration at least three to four days' notice before a proposed visit.
“These are not the issues which should come to the court.
What is required is a small SOP (standard operating procedure),” a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi observed.

Moitra, the MP from West Bengal's Krishnanagar constituency, alleged in her plea that Nadia district administration officials had evicted her from a Circuit House in August despite a room being allotted to her at the state-owned property.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the West Bengal government, told the bench that no officer had asked Moitra to vacate the premises and that all courtesies had been extended to her, according to PTI.
Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, representing Moitra, said the September 1 circular was targeted at her.
He also said that, according to protocol, an MP ranks higher than the chief secretary.
“We would like this to be ironed out.
There should not be any inconvenience to anyone,” the bench said.

stories.headline: Supreme Court seeks Centre’s reply on social media age limits for children
stories.title: Supreme Court seeks Centre’s reply on social media age limits for children
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 16 : The Supreme Court on Friday issued notice to the Centre on a plea seeking a comprehensive and enforceable regulatory framework to protect children from the risks associated with social media platforms, including age-based restrictions on access and safeguards against online exploitation. A Bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi issued notice on the petition filed by The Emerald Heights International School and its Director (Academics), Siddharth Singh Girnar, and tagged it with a pending petition raising a similar issue. The apex court has listed the matter for further hearing on December 3. The petition, filed against the Union of India, the Ministry of Women and Child Development, the Ministry of Law and Justice, and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights, raises concerns over unrestricted access to commercial social media platforms by children and the alleged inadequacy of the existing legal and regulatory framework to address the risks posed by their use. The plea contends that social media platforms generally prescribe a self-declared minimum age of 13 years, which does not correspond to the protection accorded to children under Indian law. It refers to the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which recognises every person below 18 years of age as a child and provides for enhanced safeguards, including verifiable parental consent and restrictions on tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising. “The present framework remains fragmented, incomplete and inadequately operationalised,” the petition stated, arguing that there is no uniform and enforceable child-safety regime governing age verification, prevention of underage access, parental involvement and platform accountability. The petitioners have claimed that children are increasingly exposed to cyberbullying, harassment, harmful online content and unwanted contact from strangers through social media. They have also raised concerns over sleep deprivation, diminished concentration, anxiety, low self-esteem and declining academic engagement associated with prolonged social media use. The plea further stated that parents have expressed concerns over their children's excessive phone use, late-night exposure, online interactions and the risk of bullying, grooming and exploitation, while finding it difficult to supervise or restrict access to such platforms. The petition has sought directions to the Centre and the authorities concerned to formulate and notify a dedicated regulatory framework providing for reliable, proportionate and privacy-preserving age verification, graded and age-appropriate access, restrictions on harmful content and mandatory privacy settings for accounts belonging to children. It has also sought safeguards against grooming, sexual solicitation, cyberbullying, harassment and the circulation of intimate or private images, including effective reporting mechanisms, prompt removal of harmful material and preservation of evidence in accordance with law. In the alternative, the petitioners have sought directions to prescribe and enforce restrictions on children's creation and use of social media platforms if other safeguards are found insufficient to address the risks. --IANS

A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi took note of the plea filed by Emerald Heights International School and its director of academics, Siddharth Singh Girnar, and issued notices to the ministries of women and child development and law and justice, and the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR). The bench tagged the plea, filed by Vaibhav Choudhary, with a pending petition and listed it for hearing on December 7. stories.headline: Cabinet approves ₹2,010 cr bonus for over 11 lakh railway employees
stories.title: Cabinet approves ₹2,010 cr bonus for over 11 lakh railway employees
stories.summary: The payment of PLB, which is disbursed each year before the Durga Puja/Dusshera holidays, acts as an incentive to motivate the railway employees
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'cabinet approves' in title weight 44
candidate gate: no category but HIGH+ priority -> allowed
article_sentences: Ahead of Dussehra and Deepavali festivals, the Union Cabinet on Wednesday approved Productivity Linked Bonus of 78 days for 11,40,770 railway employees, amounting to ₹2009.61 crore.

The payment of PLB, which is disbursed each year before the Durga Puja/Dusshera holidays, acts as an incentive to motivate the railway employees for working towards improvement in the performance of the Railways, the government said.
“The maximum amount payable per eligible railway employee is ₹17,951 for 78 days,” it added.

The bonus will be paid to various categories of Railway staff like track maintainers, loco pilots, train managers (Guards), station masters, supervisors, technicians, technician helpers, pointsmen, ministerial staff and other Group C staff.
“The performance of Railways in the year 2025-26 was very good.
Railways loaded a record cargo of 1670 million tonnes and carried nearly 7.41 billion Passengers,” it said.
